newsitem.title: INDIA: India gives its economy mixed report card.
newsitem.headline: India gives its economy mixed report card.

text.p: India on Tuesday gave its economy mixed grades and said more free-market reforms were needed to compete with developing powerhouses like China.

In an annual report on the state of the economy, the centre-left government said a liberalisation programme launched in 1991 had placed India, with seven percent average annual growth, among the top 10 economic performers in the world.
But the future is clouded by infrastructure bottlenecks, rising inflation and sluggish exports, it said in the Economic Survey for the 1996/97 fiscal year ending on March 31.
The survey's pitch for more reforms reflected the economic orthodoxy popular in the Finance Ministry but irksome to left-wing parties in Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fractious 15-party coalition.
Economic nationalists in the coalition's communist parties have been fighting to keep in place trade and investment restrictions which protect many domestic firms.

But the survey said the broad prescription of open borders and markets which was anathema to India during more than four decades of socialism after independence in 1947 had been largely swallowed by the political class.

"With the growing participation of virtually the entire spectrum of political opinion in the reform process," the survey said, "there is a good prospect that a higher growth rate would become a permanent feature of the economy."

Marshalling pages of statistics, the government said economic growth, trade and savings had greatly improved in the past five years. The balance of payments had strengthened, and the fiscal deficit as a share of gross domestic product had fallen to 5.8 percent in 1995/96 from 8.3 percent in 1990/91.

But it spotted clouds on the horizon. The performance of infrastructure sectors -- mainly electricity, crude oil and steel -- has been poor, while the "parlous financial state" of many public utilities increased the risk of crises, it said.
A slowdown in new phone connections suggested the government needs to dismantle controls over that sector, it said.

In one of the report's more controversial recommendations, it said the burgeoning debt that the government owes state-controlled oil companies due to petroleum subsidies called out for a phasing out of price controls.

It also said domestic oil prices had to be brought in line with higher world prices to prevent the oil subsidy bill, estimated to reach 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion) at the end of March, from ballooning out of control.
Left-wing parties, fearful of the impact that a second rise in petroleum product prices since last July would have on the poor, have been resisting a looming adjustment.

The report lauded a reduction in the current account deficit as a share of gross domestic product to 1.4 percent in 1996/97 from the previous year. But it said export growth had slumped and aggressive foreign sales promotion was needed.
Citing recurrent power failures in the capital New Delhi, the government said roadblocks to increased private investment in electricity generation needed to be lifted.
It said foreign direct investment had risen to $1.7 billion in April-December 1996 from $1.5 billion in the same period in 1995, but was far below the target of $10 billion a year.
"We must learn from the pragmatic nationalism of China which received about $40 billion of investment in 1996 and expects to attract more in 1997," it said.
